utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, is the Defence ready to continue the cross-examination of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we are, indeed, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Tucker. Please be seated. Mr. Tucker, may I remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration that you gave at the beginning of the your testimony.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Cross-examined by Mr. Piletta-Zanin: [Continued]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We are perhaps going to go to an area where we stopped yesterday, but before that, I would like you to give us some answers as to the dates that you were supposed to look up in your notebook. Could you please do that?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The date of the attack on the marketplace that we were discussing yesterday was around the 6th of February of 1994. The 6th of February, 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second date was the date of the news conference, press conference, called at Kosevo hospital, which was then fired upon, and that date was around the 9th of December, 1992. And the reason I am not specific about the date is that I only heard about it about 14 days later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. Now, have you had any knowledge in the same vein as to what you have told us earlier? Did you have any knowledge about the facts that the Sarajevo forces, that is, BH forces, would have fired a little bit earlier, a little bit before the arrival of a diplomatic convoy to Sarajevo, and which was escorted by one of the negotiators? Now, that was "escorting."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter apologises. Escorting one of the negotiators.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you like me to rephrase the question?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have any knowledge, sir, of a situation where Sarajevo forces fired not at a convoy but just before a convoy arrived in Sarajevo. This was in Sarajevo. This was escorting one of the negotiators in relation to the peace plan.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, you spoke yesterday of ceasefires; do you remember?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, is it true that General Galic, who is here today, was himself involved in these negotiations in order to obtain a ceasefire?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Sir, do you know the abbreviation "TEZ" mean, please?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Total Exclusion Zone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that not perhaps a Total Exclusion Zone?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Total Exclusion Zone.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know, sir, in relation to this Total Exclusion Zone, and we are talking about heavy weapons, General Galic was also in charge of these negotiations or he took an active part in the negotiations?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that General Galic was involved with negotiations at the mixed military working group, and those negotiations were on a daily basis, the business of Brigadier General Cordy-Simpson, who was General Morillon's Chief of Staff. It was only when they came to the signing and final conclusions that General Morillon became involved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. But General Galic was quite active on the level of these discussions; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, is it true to say that one of the negotiations, one of the objectives of these negotiations, was to either withdraw completely or have the heavy weapons, as many heavy weapons as possible, to have them removed to the peripheric areas of Sarajevo on one hand, and on the other hand, to place them under UN control?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you for your answer, sir. Now, sir, we spoke of a ceasefire plan and a plan of withdrawing heavy weapons from Sarajevo. Could we consider that at the time that you have known the plan of the Main Staff, if there was one, if there was a plan, consisted, in fact, of whatever the reasons to look for, to look to find a ceasefire and to promote peace?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, I would like us to examine some slightly more technical questions. You know, no doubt, of the existence of an ad hoc military commission. First of all, is it true that there was commissions, there were mixed or joint commissions in Sarajevo at the time of your stay in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. The commission I am talking about is called the mixed military working group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us from which period, from what time, were these groups established?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mixed military working group was started by headquarters Sector Sarajevo before the arrival of General Morillon. It was then actively picked up by General Morillon and particularly by General Cordy-Simpson and it carried on its work throughout the time that I was in Bosnia. And I do not know what happened specifically to that, to the mixed military working group, after the 31st of March, 1993, when I left Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, would you be able to tell us briefly what were the duties or the functions of the -- of this commission, the general outlines?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first point is to understand why the mixed military working group was started and that was because, at the highest level, when politicians were involved, it seemed to be impossible to make any progress. Therefore, the decision was made by the United Nations, Sector Sarajevo, to speak with the military commanders one step down from the political leaders, hence, mixed military working group. The tasks of the mixed military working group were, firstly, to try and achieve a ceasefire around Sarajevo; secondly, to try and achieve a ceasefire across all of Bosnia; thirdly, to try and achieve a freedom of movement into and out of the city; and lastly, to achieve the removal of weapons - you referred to heavy weapons - from around Sarajevo. And sir, there is one more thing: It was also to repair and improve the utilities, in other words, water, gas, electricity, supply into the city and to the surrounding areas, in order to make the life of the citizens more bearable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a clarification. Sir, first of all, thank you for your answer. You said that one of the tasks, and last but not least task, was to withdraw the heavy weapons from around Sarajevo. Could you tell us in and around Sarajevo, withdraw heavy weapons in and around Sarajevo, so you were saying inside Sarajevo and from outside Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now sir, this commission, was it also tasked of missions of more technical nature, for instance, conducting expert investigations, for instance, in mortar firing?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not responsible for the actual conduct of the investigations. In a more general sense, it was responsible for investigating occasions where the ceasefire was broken and in order to try and resolve how and why the ceasefire was broken, in order to assist both sides with maintaining the discipline necessary in order to ensure that ceasefires were adhered to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Do you know, sir, who was specifically informed when there was an incident? When an incident occurred like the one that you mentioned, who was informed?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The source of the information could be varied. One source was the group of United Nations military observers who were positioned on strategic points of view --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no, sir. I am sorry. I apologise. I am not asking the question about the source of information. What I was saying is that when an investigation is launched, who would be informed, for instance, on the Serb side, on the Bosnian side, and so on?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The participants in the mixed military working group would be informed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that always the case?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, it was always the case. And the way that information was passed when people were not actually at the mixed military working group, that I cannot speak about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, I would like us to come back to some other elements. Does the name of operation code name "Oxygen" mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is something that I recall. I am not entirely sure what it relates to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I tell you sir, that there were oxygen bottles that were allegedly filled with oxygen and they were delivered to hospitals, does that ring any bells?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That does ring a bell, and there were complaints by the Bosnian Serb side that that had happened, and I would have to look in my notes to remember more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Sir, as far as you can recall, is it true that in fact what happened is that gunpowder was delivered, was hidden in oxygen bottles? Is that what we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe it was gunpowder. The information that I had was that it was explosives for making mortar bombs with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you are the expert in artillery so I will take your word. But, in any case, it was explosives, we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know if these complaints achieved anything, was there any particular procedure?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not at the forum where these complaints were made. What I do know is that General Cordy-Simpson took some steps in order to try and ensure that the next load of oxygen bottles, when they came in, were inspected by United Nations personnel before they were shipped and brought into Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know, sir, of an operation code name "Container"?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Not containers that were positioned in order to protect people from fire.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall such a name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, do you know of an operation code name "Korat"?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it is not a name I am familiar with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, yesterday, you said in relation to two journalists who were present when mortar mobiles fired, that they were told to leave the city without delay, and I think that you added something like "for their safety." Do you remember that you said that?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. What did you mean by saying these three words, "for their safety"?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time in December 1992, there was a struggle for power going on inside Sarajevo. There were some very radical elements and who had been responsible for considerable difficulties, both to the ceasefires, both to the United Nations, to the authorities in Sarajevo. And the difficulties they had been causing was black market. They were terrorising some of the civilians in certain areas and they had been carrying out attacks in various areas. The authorities were trying to clamp down on them and there were -- there was a period of roadblocks by the police all around the inside of the city in order to try and clamp down on these irregulars. And the advice that I gave to these two journalists was on the basis that, inside the city, there was not what I would describe as the due situation of law and order and that with these hardliners about, they could be at risk if hardliners came to hear that they had given hard evidence about something which was very sensitive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer, sir. You said that they could be at risk. Should I understand that could they have been killed?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what I believed possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Should I understand, sir, that it wasn't really in their capacity as witnesses that they were at risk, but they were particularly at risk because they were witnesses who were journalists?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I believe that they were at risk because of the specific incident that they had witnessed, not because they were just journalists in general.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I would like us to continue along this line of questioning. We spoke at length about the crime and the power struggle. Yesterday you told us about somebody called "Juka," and do you remember that, sir?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us the full name of that person?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it is Juka Boje [phoen]. I can't -- phonetically, I am probably incorrect, but that is what I --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does the name of Juka Prazina mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prazina does not mean anything to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please tell us who was this Juka that we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Juka that I am talking about is -- rather, was a -- a criminal who General Mladic complained to General Morillon about, saying that UNPROFOR had helped move this person into and out of Sarajevo. And General Morillon declared to General Mladic that, yes, he was aware who this Juka was, that he was a criminal, and that as far as General Morillon was aware, that Juka was in gaol. After the meeting, because I was not aware before the meeting of who Juka was, General Morillon told me that Juka was a petty gangster in Sarajevo before the war, and when the fighting started, he had used his gangster connections and had organised amongst a section of the population resistance against the Bosnian Serb force attacks, and in so doing, had achieved a sort of hero status. That had initially been of use to the nascent authorities in Sarajevo who had no organised military force with which to resist the attacks from the Bosnian Serb forces. However, once the Sarajevo force or authorities began to exercise power, Juka insisted on carrying on independently and not subjecting himself to the discipline and authority of the Sarajevo authorities. He then became more of a liability than an asset, and he was captured by the Sarajevo authorities and deported from Sarajevo. And when General Morillon and General Mladic had their conversation, which was the first meeting that General Morillon and Mladic had, General Morillon said that he believed that he was in gaol somewhere in the -- somewhere in the south-west of Bosnia. I can't recall the name of the city.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Since this Juka was a warlord, do you know where his headquarters was?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you know if this warlord who had organised a private militia, or at least of a private type, had several areas in the town, had several headquarters in the town?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I am aware of is that there were several areas within the city which were dominated by particular gangsters at the early days of the siege of Sarajevo. Which particular areas they were, the headquarters Sector Sarajevo was aware of, but it was not something which I involved myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, sir, I am going to come back to the question of the explosive that was delivered and the information that you gave us of the control or the checking that was imposed by the UN on the oxygen bottles that were brought into the town. It is true that the bottle or bottles that were found containing gunpowder were supposed to go to a hospital outside of Sarajevo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding was that they were -- that the explosives were inside oxygen bottles which were being brought from outside Sarajevo into Sarajevo, to hospital inside Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, sir, if we bring explosive into Sarajevo, we assume that this is for the reason that it is to be used?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, in your capacity as a -- practically an expert, an artillery officer, how would it be possible to have a workshop or a factory to manufacture projectiles, projectiles that would be used for mortar? Would it be possible?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would absolutely be possible. If you gave me a garage workshop, I would be able to do it myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you are saying to me that a very small building, say a garage, with some tools, could be sufficient to have manufacturing of this kind of projectiles. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, should I also conclude from your answer that at the end of the day, if we have all the elements, if we have the powder, if we have the location, if we have the tools, then it would be possible to manufacture almost anywhere such ammunition? So, my question: It would be possible to manufacture such units which would be able to manufacture ammunition?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Providing you had the know-how and the steel as well, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, as far as the know-how is concerned, is it true that an artillery officer who has your competence would be able to give the necessary instructions for making such a factory?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not call it a factory. I would call it a DIY assembly of mortars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. But your answer is yes?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now sir, do you know if at a given time there were such workshops, in order not to call them factories, near or inside the PTT building?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That, I have no knowledge of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you have any knowledge of any sites that would have been manufacturing such products in and around Sarajevo? In Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: In Sarajevo. Interpreter apologises.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that that activity carried on inside Sarajevo, as well as collecting unexploded Serb shells, which were sawn open. The explosive inside was melted and poured out in order to be used for home-made mortar bombs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, if I understand you well, there was a para-industrial structure in Sarajevo which made it possible to remelt metals to be used for cartridges?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not to remelt metals, it was to liquefy the explosives inside Serb shells so you could then pour the explosive out, because it was otherwise dangerous to take out. That is the technique that you use.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. In practice, there was a structure to recuperate, to renew armaments, BH armaments, in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, because they were surrounded and they were being attacked and they had no other way of defending themselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am taking note of this, what you have just said, and thank you, Witness. Now, I would like to come back to another one of your statements about an attack which took place at 400 metres, more or less, from the residence. Do you remember it, yesterday, on page 2 -- page 7, line 2, you spoke of a distance of 400 metres which made it possible for you to see it?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Point of clarification, Witness, and I must say that we have testimonies that go in that direction. Is it technically correct to say that an armament such as a mortar is not as precise, as accurate, as an arm of direct fire and that, consequently, the use of a mortar involves necessarily a margin of error in regards to targets and that one which is greater than in the case of direct fire?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just to indicate that in the transcript it says, "no audible response" to the previous questions about the 400 metres. Perhaps that could be reflected what the witness was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it was the question whether the witness remembered that he spoke of a distance of 400 metres which made it possible for you to see it. Your answer was in the affirmative, as far as I remember.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, now I would like to come back to this margin of error. Some witnesses told us that with a mortar, we speak of a zone of error which can amount to 400 metres on targets to the extent to which there may be a long fire, a short fire, and then a shot to the target. Would you say that this is, in principle, correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible. The function of the accuracy of a mortar relates to whether it is a heavy mortar or a light mortar and over the range at which it is fired. But, yes, a 400 metre error is certainly possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, now I would like to submit to you a document which relates to your -- to your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what the number is. Can we please verify the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...tell us where we are in the numbering of the Defence exhibits.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are at D131.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: 31 is the last one?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it the next one to come or is it the last one used? The next one to come.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The next one to come is D132.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I shall give it to you, Witness. I shall give you a certain number of documents. We will begin by Exhibit D132, and I would like to ask you if you could certify if you recognise this type of document. Witness, do you recognise that type of document?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The structure of the document is fairly similar to the form of the daily sit-reps from HQ Sector Sarajevo and the headquarters, BH Command, but --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I am interrupting you because you are in the -- saying the right thing. It is a report of that kind. Could you please read out the date which is in the middle of the document under item 7.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thursday, 7 January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, do we agree that this is the date that you mentioned which corresponds to the Orthodox Christmas?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Could you please read the first line of item A?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Combat and shelling activity not specified."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness. Now, we assume that what we have above corresponds to January 6th. Would you please read the first line or the second line, even the second line of point 1446.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The city had been quiet as Serbs began preparing to celebrate the Serb Orthodox Christmas. Sarajevo radio said heavy guns opened fire during the night around the Parliament building south-west of the city centre -- "

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please read more slowly.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "The city had been quiet as Serbs began preparing to celebrate the Serb Orthodox Christmas. Sarajevo radio said heavy guns opened fire during the night around the Parliament building south-west of the city centre and that there was sporadic small-arm fire in the same area."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Witness, now with the assistance of Madam Usher, I would like to submit to you a document carrying the number 133. I would like to ask you, now that you have it in front of you, to read the first line of point A.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that point A for the 5th of January --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [In English] No, for the 6th.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Military active combat and shelling activity. The city was reported quiet in the early hours as Serbs began preparing for the Orthodox Christmas."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellent. Thank you. Now I would like to give you --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know if Mr. Waespi -- numbers 134 and 135. Could the usher kindly give those documents to the witness. We will do it together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very quickly, Witness, could you please look at, in respect of document 134, what the text says under "A," combat and shelling activity?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is for the 24th of December, 1992: "Military activity, combat and shelling activity. UN officers estimated that about 400 artillery, tank and mortar shells exploded in the city."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness read more slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "UN officers estimated that about 400 artillery, tank, and mortar shells exploded in the city."

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I would like you to do the same in relation to the next document, which has to do with December 22nd -- 25th, 1992.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Section A: "Combat and shelling activity. Shelling was reportedly reduced on Christmas Day, but several large explosions hit the centre of Sarajevo in the morning."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Witness, now let us focus on other points. You mentioned in your testimony of yesterday that the Serb forces fired during the night at people who were crossing the airport runway and that they caused, on a daily basis, between 5, 20 or 30 victims. This is what you mentioned yesterday, if you remember.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned that you were certain of what you said because you possessed such information from the very mouth of the colonel who was then in charge of the French Battalion at the airport, [redacted]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the residency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me when?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it would have been around the end of January, beginning of February, I think, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this figure of 5 to 30 victims, casualties, on a daily basis, was this -- was the colonel that we were discussing, the person who told you this?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was mentioned in the context of the casualty rate which the colonel's battalion was also suffering.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise. What language did the colonel speak in?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: French.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, I apologise, but could you please answer my question in French, now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, you are requested to answer in French. Of course, you only have to do so if you speak the French language in such a way that you think that you could answer in French.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is possible, I can speak French, yes. I am completely capable of speaking in French and I understood almost everything that you said in French.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Certainly, and definitely. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am going to repeat my question, Witness. And considering that I know that you speak French, are you absolutely certain, do you categorically say, that this colonel mentioned these figures to you which doesn't marry with his testimony?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said those figures to General Morillon in my presence, in French, and it was during the heaviest period of the people trying to run across the airport.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I can just take note of what you said. Do you know, Witness, if you knew him who was a certain name called Caco?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I am not -- I don't recall the name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I am going to have you look at a document numbered 136, with the assistance of Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: One point, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: As a matter of courtesy, before the witness is asked, I guess even shown a potential exhibit, and even more before he starts to read, let me please have a copy of the proposed exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think they are provided to you, but it is just the logistics in the courtroom that cause the problem at this very moment. But it have been solved as far as I see.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. President, there is some advice I would like to ask you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you -- is it of such a nature that you can do it in public or is there anything specific that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is some information regarding the last exhibits of which were given to me and which I read out, which I believe are pertinent to the interpretation of those exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I don't know whether we can come back to that, but considering the time and that I would like to keep to the time, I suggest that we go on to other matters and then possibly later we can come back to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the witness asked advice at this very moment. Of course, we will take that into account and measuring your time which, as you indicated, is not very much any more. So we can do it in public. What would you like to -- what advice would you like to ask us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would like to ask you whether I may say something about the way that the reports were compiled which I read out just now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you think that these are sit-reps, I think whatever clarification you would like to give, we will listen to it, but these are not sit-reps, although they may be based on sit-reps. So if it is of any relevance, please tell us. But these are not sit-reps you just read out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I believe I know where those documents came from, and they are compiled based on the UN sit-reps. The UN sit-reps are largely compiled from the reports by the United Nations military observers who were stationed around the city. And when those observers are resting and not expecting any particular activity, they do not catch the activity and do not report the activity. And I know that in a number of occasions, like, for example, the attack on the 31st of October, 1992, the observers did not catch the majority of the events. And if you were to conduct an analysis of the reports of -- by the observers, you would not get an accurate reflection of the combat activity that went on in and around Sarajevo. You would have an indication but it would not be a totally accurate one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your clarification. Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, at the end of this document, 136, we have a page which has a number, 161, and I would like you to have a look at this very last page of the document. Did you find that page?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that what it says here under column "gas" corresponds to, in your memory, to the reality which is that the fact that the infrastructures of gas distribution were not destroyed but were in operational conditions, in a state of working relatively normally?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: My understanding was that the gas supplies were turned off, either inside Bosnian Serb-held territory or in Serbia itself. There was some damage to the actual distribution system inside Sarajevo and immediately around it. But the pressure of the gas was so low, basically because it had been turned off, that very little gas came through. Sometimes the gas was opened and then higher pressure built up, but it was never for more than a couple of days at a time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, this document says that about 5.000 apartments were connected to the gas network without authorisation. Did you know about this?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have no information of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, could you please read the very last sentence of the first paragraph under "standard of living."

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Pumps at -- "

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [In English] No, no, no. "Standard of living." At the top of the page, please.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "UNHCR can however"?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "There is no starvation among the population."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. I would like to go to another subject in the few minutes that we have left. Sir, you said that you were present when there were shots -- there were indiscriminate shots fired. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Sir, could you tell us a location, for instance, a specific location where such firing occurred?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It happened in many occasions along the routes from the residency to headquarters Sector Sarajevo and between headquarters Sector Sarajevo and the airport.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, you are talking about a route. Is it true --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you were talking about a route. Is it true that in military technique, communication route, an act of communication, a route could be considered a military -- legitimate military target in times of war?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not the route which is the military target, it is that which uses the route.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you saying that a bridge would not be a military target?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: A bridge would be a military target if logistics were being carried across it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. And so a bridge being part of a route, of a road, so if we say that the road, if it has military purpose, would then be a military target, right?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The circumstances would depend.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. I am talking about the principle.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, could you please give us an example in a city, in one location where you were present when there was a shelling that could be described as indiscriminate shelling?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I was at the residency, on many days, I could hear shells landing within 300, 400 metres of the residency and we sometimes had to take cover inside the residency because shells were landing close enough to make us take cover.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. But, could you please tell me a location, an address, a precise address?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot tell you an address because, if I could, then I would not be here today because the shell would have landed on me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you could have passed by the location the following day, you could have seen the traces of the shell and we still would have had the pleasure of seeing you here today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just three more minutes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I said I would strictly keep you to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, sir, simply, could you, before this Chamber, categorically exclude that there was no mobile military target at that location, nor possibly one of these HQs that you did not know of, that you did not know of their existence?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I can say is --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. My question, I am sorry, is very simple: Could you exclude the possibility, categorically exclude, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Sir, I would, in the same line of questioning, I would like to ask you to tell me if you know the person called Lars-Eric Wahlgren?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if this person said in Sarajevo there were the following: [In English] "A large number of military installation and therefore it would have been very difficult to have made it a demilitarised zone."

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Very last question. Sir, in relation to the incident of Prime Minister Mr. Turajlic who arrived at the airport, first of all, we have testimony of high-rank officers that it was not always possible to have surveillance and control of all the members of an army. Is that what you could confirm?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That seems an obvious statement to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, to the Defence as well, and I thank you for it. Thank you very much. Now, as far as the incident is concerned, do you know that the man who fired these shots was a man who was, in fact, mentally disturbed?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not know that. That is not what General Mladic told General Morillon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, your time is over. You said your very last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed. Indeed, it is this one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you yourself, sir, were you there at that time and did you attend this event?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean when General Mladic told General Morillon --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I mean the actual incident at the airport.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not. I was at the residency at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That was your last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any need to re-examine the witness, Mr. Waespi?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, very briefly and with your leave, my colleague, Mark Ierace, would add a couple of questions if that would be allowed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We allowed that several times to the Defence. It is the first time you asked for it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. Re-examined by Mr. Waespi:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, I just want to ask you to keep on reading of a small number of statements you had to read out by the Defence. The first one was the potential Defence exhibit - I think it was the last one which was shown to you - the cover page carries the UN symbol, and if you can go to the last page, it started, "standard of living." And you were asked to read out the first sentence, "There is no -- " I quote: "There is no starvation among the population." So could you please keep on reading.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I continue: "They survive on what the human relief organisations give them and on what they grow themselves in gardens and even balconies."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Tucker. Perhaps it is of assistance if you can go to the bottom of the page and try to read out perhaps the author and the dates of the reference.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The author is Captain Timerman, a United Nations military observer from headquarters Sarajevo, on the 11th of September, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next page I would like you to refer to is potential Defence Exhibit 132. If the witness could be provided, in fact, with all the exhibits that the Defence had given him. The first one would be number 132. You have been asked, I think, about the top narrative of events number 1446. I would like you to read out the next paragraph, which is 1447.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read 1447: "Sarajevo radio reported intense shelling of the Novi Grad district. Over 50 shells were reported to have fallen on Stari Grad late in the afternoon and in the evening. It said that the Hrasno district was shelled by mortars, tanks and anti-aircraft fire. Street fighting was also reported in the Dobrinja and Vojnicko Polje districts."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tucker. And then on the same page you were asked about the 7th of January, 1993, and you read out about combat --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just have to interrupt because it did not appear in the French translation, that Vojnicko Polje, the army field district.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that is corrected now. Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were asked about the part, I quote: "combat and shelling activity," and then you read out "not specified." Can I ask you to read out what it says a few lines further down about casualties.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Casualties: The BiH Public Health Ministry reported that two people were killed and 25 wounded on this day."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like you to go to the next page that is the potential Exhibit number 135. You were asked here to talk about military activity. If you go down further that page to number 1395, it starts with, I quote, "several large explosions." If you could read this part out, please.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read 1395: "Several large explosions rocked the centre of the Sarajevo in the morning. Sarajevo radio said Serb-fired shells landed in the compound of the Kosevo hospital near Morillon's residence."

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. Now Mr. Ierace has a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Re-examined by Mr. Ierace:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, you told us this morning that you consulted some notes in order to determine the date of the incident that you discussed with Mr. Itani. Could you tell us, firstly, what notes you consulted in order to determine that date?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I consulted some notes at the back of a diary which I held when I was in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When were you in Srebrenica, between what dates?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Srebrenica from around the 6th of -- 5th of 6th of March, 1992 through to the end of March 1992, the 30th or the 31st of March. Sorry, 1993. The 31st of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Do you have that note with you in court today?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it back at your hotel?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could just summarise what you have told us. As I understand it, you consulted some notes at the back of a diary which you held when you were in Srebrenica, and you were in Srebrenica from the 5th or 6th of March, 1993 until the 30th or 31st of March, 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you believe that you made that entry that you consulted while you were in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any indication with the note as to when, that is, the date, that you made the entry?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't believe so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say that the person you had the conversation with was Mr. Itani, was that --

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not with Major Itani that I had the conversation. The conversation was with a British Army sergeant major who had been involved with the investigation together with Major Itani, and it was this British sergeant Major who I met in headquarters 1st UK Armoured Division in Germany in, I think, late 1994/1995.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the name of the British Army sergeant major?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember his name. He was the -- he was an artillery intelligence sergeant major who had been deployed with one of the Cymbeline [phoen] mortar located radars in Sarajevo and he was an expert in the technique of examining shell craters in order to identify from where a shell had been fired, in order that counterbattery bombardment could be carried out.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Are you saying then that this British Army sergeant major told you that Major Itani, the Canadian artillery officer, had carried out an investigation?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that -- the British Army sergeant major showed me a report, a copy of this report, from that event, and my recollection is that he had carried out that, he, the British Army sergeant major, had carried out an investigation together with Major Itani.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you meet Major Itani when you were in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was he at one stage a member of General Morillon's staff?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was it, if you know it, that Major Itani left Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. He was in Sarajevo when I left.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that this British officer showed you a copy of a report, and I think you said a report that the British Army officer had been involved in, in terms of the investigation. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember anything as to the nature of the report, in particular, whether it was prepared by, or for, any particular agency?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was prepared for the UN.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what particular agency of the UN?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: A military agency. It was not a civilian agency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To your knowledge, I think you have referred to two UN military agencies in your evidence so far, being UNPROFOR and another agency which perhaps is also a part of UNPROFOR, that is the UNMOs. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of any other UN military agency that was operating in Sarajevo at any stage of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it therefore follow that the agency involved in the report had to have been UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be my assumption.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note the time. I wish to obtain a document to show the witness in re-examination. Would that be convenient?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we would first have the break and see whether there are any additional questions by the Bench. But after the break, you could start to show a document to the witness. Of course, we do not know what document it is, but you have an opportunity to find it over the next half hour. We will adjourn until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace -- Mr. Piletta-Zanin, yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, very quickly. You will have noted a few moments ago that we had not spoke about the second incident or the first incident, depending on how you look at it, regarding the market in our examination of the witness. Now, if the Prosecution wishes ask new questions of the witness in relation to this, the Defence reserves the right to respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Within certain time limits, if new evidence comes up, then you will have an opportunity to respond. Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, in relation to that, it is my submission that indeed the Defence did cross-examine about that issue, but in any event, I will continue, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I ask that the witness be shown Exhibit P2261. That is the document which has already been tendered into evidence. In fact, I think it is P2261A. That is the English version, and B is the translation into B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the extent -- we don't hear the counsel. We didn't hear what the counsel said. He hadn't his microphone switched on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please put the document on the ELMO, since we have no copies at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, I think part of the document is on the ELMO at the moment. If you require an opportunity to leaf through the document in order to answer my question, please say so. My question is: Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recognise neither of the documents which have been placed in front of me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have two documents in front of you?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. In any event, in relation to the British officer that you met and whose name you don't recall, can you assist us with any further recollection you may have as to his identity?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe that this is not the event which I was talking about. I do not see his name anywhere on this and this does not look familiar. It must have been the marketplace attack in, I believe it was August 1995 that I am referring to -- that I referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that the document be returned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please assist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yesterday, you were asked this question and gave this answer in cross-examination: Question: "Did you, sir, however, see even smaller elements that would correspond to private personal vehicles, are they passenger vehicle like Golf, for instance, where there would be mortars mounted on top of them? They would have been placed inside vehicles and with which small units could move around that shoot for a while and then move, then withdraw. Do you know anything about this?" "Answer: Yes, I know that that happened. I did not see it myself, but I read reports from our intelligence people who had had reports from soldiers on the ground who had seen such vehicles and such people."

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I would like to ask to give us the quotation, precise quotation, and the line. Because you will remember yesterday we had asked for a rectification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was wondering what question would come, so if it would relate to that correction then. But it is as Mr. Ierace reads it. That is how it was in the transcript yesterday. I have that very clear in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will then ask you to rectify it correct, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, I think the intervention of Mr. Piletta-Zanin relates to a -- well, some difficulties in the translation yesterday which do not appear clearly in the transcript. So I will wait until you have put your question to the witness, and if it is in relation to that problem, I might intervene, but I will first let you go.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, at a later point, there was some clarification elicited from you as to your source or sources of information. My question does not relate to that. In the question you were asked, there were a number of separate propositions and your answer did not deal with those separate propositions. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, if I may intervene. If you are pointing at the difference between mortars mounted on a lorry or a small truck or inside a car, "inside the car" was a rectification for a wrong translation. So the question and the testimony of the witness was about mortar in a personal vehicle. I don't know whether you are --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I won't take it any further, Mr. President, if that has been clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was the issue that I think Mr. Piletta-Zanin --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly what I had thought and I am at the -- always at the disposal of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...of the question which was made after Mr. Piletta-Zanin asked for a better translation. So inside a personal vehicle, and not mounted on the back of a small truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. One remaining issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, you gave evidence in cross-examination as to the area of accuracy of mortars, and the figure of 400 metres was mentioned. What are the relevant aspects of the firing of mortars to the accuracy of mortars?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are a number of factors. If I start first with positioning a mortar rigidly in one position so it is aimed at one spot and then fire a whole series of shells from that same mortar aimed at one spot, those shells will land in a long ellipse in the line that the mortar is pointing. The length of the ellipse will be about eight times the width of the ellipse, and the length of that ellipse depends upon the range at which the mortar is firing. And roughly speaking, if you take the ratio of the range together with the size of the mortar, in other words, a light mortar, a 60-millimetre mortar, fired at the maximum range which is about 500, 600 metres, you will have quite a wide spread. Whereas a heavy mortar fired at what is a much closer range will have a much smaller ellipse. It will be more accurate. The second aspect is how accurate your aim is. The first aspect is a technical aspect. The second aspect is how accurate your aim is. The difficulty with mortars, as for artillery, is obviously that from the position you are firing, you can rarely actually see the targets. So you have to carry out calculations about where to point the mortar or the artillery gun. And your accuracy in selecting that can vary tremendously, and that is the biggest cause of inaccuracy of mortars and artillery guns. Now, a mortar, the sight system on the mortar is much more coarse than the sight system on an artillery gun, which is much more precise. And when the gun fires, it comes back into the same position much more reliably. So it is the sighting of the weapon which can cause errors. I have seen errors in training of two kilometres. That's not because it's a mortar, a poor gun. That is simply because it was aimed at the wrong direction. If you add in the third factor, which is weather, because the winds -- and the mortar fire is very high, unlike an artillery shell which is much flatter, they are subject to the winds, and again to give you an example, on training, I have seen shells moved just by the wind about 600, 700 metres from where they were meant to land.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are very inaccurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further intervention from my side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Some one or more questions will be put to you by Judge Nieto-Navia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Yesterday, you mentioned as part of the tactics of the BSA the house-to-house fighting. Could you elaborate a little bit on that?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The house-to-house fighting tactics, the BSA used in the Otes and Stup areas, were carried out by regular, that is, professional, well-trained infantry. House-to-house fighting is a very difficult activity to carry out competently. It is much easier to defend, with little training, than it is to attack. To attack successfully, you have to do a lot of training. I have done this myself. The technique is where Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you have to identify which the next house is that you want to attack. You need to bring it under fire from several other points so that you have got covering fire. You then bring people under the covering fire to the outside of the building. You then enter the building, preferably through a wall because you don't want to come in through the window or the door, and I am now talking about the training that undergo in the British Army. You then enter the building and clear it room by room, and it takes a lot of ammunition, a lot of discipline, a lot of communication and a lot of training. And the reports which came to us from the United Nations military observers and from headquarters Sector Sarajevo indicated that these were the tactics which were being employed by the BSA in the attacks around Stup-Otes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: How can the civilian population be affected by that?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very badly. Anybody living, it would be virtually impossible to live as a civilian in an area where that kind of fighting is going on. You would not survive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Yesterday, we saw the agreement between the military command creating some corridors for freedom of movement. I would like to know if those corridors are the same so-called "blue routes."

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, those are different. The blue roads are routes from way down to the south -- to the south and south-west of Sarajevo, leading up to Sarajevo and into Sarajevo. By memory, it was roughly, 20, 30, 40 kilometres long. Whereas the corridors that I am talking about which the mixed military working group was dealing with in early December 1992, were much smaller corridors around Sarajevo airport. I can give you more detail. I can sketch roughly what those corridors were, if you like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: No, I don't think that is necessary. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge El Mahdi also has one or more questions to you. JUDGE EL MAHDI: Thank you, Mr. President. [Interpretation] In relation to what you have told us about firing coming from the surroundings of the Kosevo hospital, you told us that you received information from two sources. Firstly, from a sergeant, a British sergeant, and then from journalists. Was it a single incident or was it something which was reproduced covering firing involving against the hospital from the surroundings?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is -- it was a complex situation. The sergeant told me about one specific incident that he saw with his own eyes. The sergeant also told me that he believed that that activity was carrying on from Kosevo hospital, in other words, that firing out of the grounds of Kosevo hospital was taking place. Because on a number of occasions -- because he delivered fuel twice a week to Kosevo hospital. On a number of occasions, he was halted by Bosniaks a short distance away from the hospital and told to wait, and then he heard firing. And then he was allowed to proceed to the hospital, and there was nothing there. It was that sergeant's supposition that firing from out of the hospital had taken place. The press told me about an incident when shelling had happened of Kosevo hospital which they witnessed from close hand, and my sergeant said that he believed that firing from Kosevo hospital had happened shortly before that. It is not something that I witnessed first-hand. It is my belief and supposition from these various sources that firing by mobile Bosniak mortars from within the grounds of Kosevo hospital was something that happened a lot more than once. Whether it happened daily or once a week or -- that, I cannot say. The only other thing that I can say is that we, that General Morillon, tackled the head of Kosevo hospital, asking him, "Why do you allow this to happen? Why do you not protest to the Presidency or to the ABiH?" And he denied any knowledge of that happening. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Yes. When you say, "from out of the hospital," you don't mean from the hospital itself, but from the surroundings of the hospital? It is not from the hospital. The shooting did not come from the hospital itself or from vehicles that may have been parked in the area of the hospital, the surrounding area of the hospital?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kosevo hospital is not one single building. It is a whole complex of buildings, and between those buildings there are parking areas, grass areas. And when I say the firing was from Kosevo hospital, I mean it was from those areas between the buildings of Kosevo hospital. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Was it the only hospital in Sarajevo or were there other hospitals in Sarajevo, too?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were other hospitals in Sarajevo as well. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] As far as you know, were the other hospitals also used in the same manner, that is to say, the surrounded -- that firing would come from the surrounding area of those hospitals or was it only the case of the surrounding area of the Kosevo hospital that firing was carried out in the other hospitals, too?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must answer in several steps. The first step is to say that I have no knowledge of such firing from the proximity of other hospitals in Sarajevo. Secondly, the other hospitals in Sarajevo were very different types of building. Kosevo hospital was the only hospital which was spread out over quite a large area. The other hospitals were solid, single buildings, with a small building next to it, maybe. So they did not lend themselves to the kind of tactic. The third thing is that the head of Kosevo hospital was known to us as a radical hardliner and was someone who we believed would have certainly supported this kind of tactic in the greater interest, as he saw it, of supporting the Bosniak cause, whereas the directors of the other hospitals were, in our view, much more medically focused and refused to have anything to do with the kind of action that the director of Kosevo hospital, in our view, participated in. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] And the other hospitals, as far as you know, were they also the object of firing, or were they spared?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no specific knowledge that they were either targeted or spared. What I do know is that in reports of firing, it was always Kosevo hospital which came up, never the other hospitals. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] You said that there were factions that were not necessarily subject to a hierarchy, subjected to a hierarchy, and that is why you advised the journalists to leave the premises, the city, in fact. I wouldn't say "to your knowledge," but according to your assumptions, the shooting that came from the surrounding area of the hospital, that came out of the hospital, was -- did it come from those that were not subordinated to the hierarchy, as one would say?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that but it is very plausible and it would be my belief that that was likely.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour. Microphone, please. Could you please switch on your microphone. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] My question relates to the gas bottle incident, that is, bottles filled with powder or material which could be used to military ends. Was this the object of an investigation by your services? Have there been any traces, any documents that would confirm that the incidents took place and who was responsible for it?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: We heard about the incident at a meeting with the directors of the hospitals of Sarajevo. When they complained or they stated to us that they were very anxious about the lack of oxygen, when we asked them, "Why is there a shortage of oxygen," they then said to us, "It is because the humanitarian aid agency which brings in the bottles of oxygen is being prevented from doing that by the Serbs." We then asked: "Why are the Serbs preventing bringing in bottles of oxygen?" And we were told that it is because they found a bottle of oxygen to contain explosives, not oxygen. That is when we became involved, and we did not carry out any investigation to this incident because it had already happened and we had not been notified about it at the time. What we did instigate was to require the humanitarian aid agency which brought in those oxygen bottles, because it was a specialised medical humanitarian agency of some kind, we requested UNHCR to ensure that we, UNPROFOR forces, were able to inspect oxygen bottles before they were brought in. We then spoke with General Mladic, to tell him that we had taken that step and would he please allow the supply of oxygen bottles into Sarajevo to be continued and not to be interrupted. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Did this result in a lifting of the restrictions in regard to oxygen supplies to the city?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: To my knowledge, it did, because we didn't hear any more requests from the directors of the hospitals for oxygen. And we, therefore, assumed that it must have been addressed and resolved. JUDGE EL MAHDI: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tucker, I have a few questions for you as well. Yesterday, you testified about firing of mortars from the Kosevo hospital grounds and you used the expression on a number of occasions and you clarified that. You also testified about shelling your own people, you remember that BiH, and you also used the expression, that you "had strong circumstantial evidence that on a number of occasions this would have happened." May I ask you to clarify whether "on a number of occasions" is the same number, or what is "a number of occasions" in this respect?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this respect, it was two occasions: One was the cemetery attack which happened before I arrived in Sarajevo and the second one was the marketplace event at which we spoke earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So it was on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two occasions, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yesterday, you told us that General Morillon asked General Mladic to stop his artillery from firing into cities and towns and at civilians. And your answer continued that "General Morillon said on many occasions -- said this on many occasions and that General Mladic usually responded by saying something along the lines of his heavy weapons being equivalent to the Bosniak infantry. His forces had few infantry but many heavy weapons, whereas the Bosniaks had a lot of infantry, but few heavy weapons." The remarks of General Morillon were about attacks on towns and civilians. The response is, if I understand your answer well, is not specifically limited to attacks on civilians but just describes a -- well, could describe a combat situation as well. I mean, if you say, we have more heavy weaponry, it doesn't mean you use it to fire on civilians. Could you elaborate a bit more on the relation between the answer? Was it an evasive answer, in your view, or was it an answer responding to attacks on civilians, so that we have to understand the answer in the sense that he would use heavy weaponry against civilians? It is not quite clear to me. Could you elaborate on that a bit more?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is multi-layered [Realtime transcript read in error "multi-led"]. I believe that General Mladic's response to General Morillon was at a number of levels.
