At the first level, Mladic was expressing his anxiety about his weakness in lack of infantry. Secondly, General Mladic was expressing frustration that the international media and international condemnation was coming for the highly-visible attacks by artillery, whereas the media were never present or never noticed when the Bosniaks carried out infantry attacks, which he then had to defend using his heavy artillery because he didn't have the infantry. At the third level, General Mladic was being -- was avoiding the question because there were two levels of activity. The first level is what I would describe as, "legitimate military activity." And by "legitimate," I mean that it is acceptable to understand two military forces fighting against each other. I am not by that implying that the fighting in Bosnia was legitimate. That is a different issue and not one that I am able to judge on. But there is a second issue which was never discussed, and that is that analysis of the targets that were used, that were fired against, indicates very strongly that the heavy artillery was not being used principally against military targets, but was being used in order to terrorise the civilian population in order to apply pressure against the local civil authorities supposed to be looking after those civilians, and to apply pressure against the Bosniak authorities. And the reason that I say that is that it is entirely illegitimate, in my view, to be using artillery or mortars which have the inaccuracies which have been described just now in order to try and attack so-called military targets consisting of one building or one vehicle or somewhere when the ability of artillery or mortar, mortars, to hit that target are negligible and the chances of that artillery or mortars of hitting the surrounding civilian houses is 99.9 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. So you say as far as the question was specifically related to the attacks on civilians, the answer was evasive. That was that part of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I apologise for interrupting. Before you move on to the next question, the transcript at page 47, line 12, has the witness saying that his answer was "multi-led." I think that should be multi-layered, "l-a-y-e-r-e-d" ending. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that is how I understood it. But I didn't look at the transcript. The last question is you have told us about one of the tasks performed was to discuss issues of restoring utilities: gas, water supply, electricity. Could you tell us whether the parties were cooperative if it came to restoring these utilities, whether both parties behaved similarly or differently? Could you elaborate a bit more on that?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Utilities were something which General Morillon considered very important, and at the meetings at which utility repair was discussed, both sides were entirely cooperative. These meetings were very complex because you needed to bring to one place, at one time, both technicians who had the right knowledge and a ceasefire that was agreed by both sides, and the technicians needed to know a safe route through the minefields in order to reach the area that they needed to carry out repairs. When we looked at what happened on the ground, the cooperation which we received from the Bosnian Serb authorities was generally of a high order. The cooperation we received from the Bosniak local commanders varied considerably, and it was our belief that in some areas where the Presidency authorities had high control, things generally went well. But there were other areas where the local commanders were radical, and from the perspective of general discipline and obedience, were unreliable, that all sorts of tricks were used in order to prevent the repairs from taking place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am trying to understand this. The supplies of water, electricity and gas, also served their own population. What was the specific reason why they would play tricks which would result in not restoring the supplies when their own population would suffer from it? Do you have any explanation about that?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do have an explanation and it is as follows: There were elements within the Bosnian leadership who believed that the only way to take back that which had been taken from them by the Bosnian Serbs, that could only happen by either international intervention in Bosnia or by the provision of arms and ammunition to Bosnia, which was not possible at that time because of the arms embargo. Those people believed that the only way to secure such international assistance was to depict the situation in Sarajevo to be so severe that the international community would be -- would be willing to intervene. Therefore, it was not in their interest to see any improvement in the situation in Sarajevo. It was not in their interest to see any -- to see the lot of the civilian population improve. To put it bluntly, the more suffering, the better because that played to the television cameras and would ultimately lead to the pressure that they wanted in order to achieve international intervention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would that be, in three words, exploitation of misery?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you say that again, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would that be, in three words, exploitation of misery?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Mr. Tucker, this concludes your testimony in this court, unless Mr. Piletta-Zanin asks permission to put additional questions to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the tradition says that I should ask your leave, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it a subject touched upon by the Bench?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I believe so, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will listen to your questions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Further cross-examination by Mr. Piletta-Zanin:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly, sir, you said earlier in page 48, line 6 and 7, that the artillery of the Serb forces was not used in principal on military targets. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to ask you a question which is the following, in three parts: Isn't it true to say that the destruction of -- most important material damage that was caused of property happened in areas like Otes. Is that a yes or a no?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Then in areas like Dobrinja, would you say yes or no?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. And in, generally speaking, in areas along confrontation lines like, for instance, the area that we mentioned earlier which is called Vojnicko Polje or military field, is that also true?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is also true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Witness, is it true to say that these destructions occurred due to artillery fire, as a principal, principally speaking?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not be able to answer that. Specifically, I would say that it would be a combination of artillery fire and what I call direct fire. To explain my language, artillery fire is indirect fire. It fires over. You do not see the target you are firing at. Whereas direct fire fires in a straight line and you can see the target you are firing at. So a tank would be direct fire, whereas artillery is indirect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So when you are talking -- when you said earlier about artillery fire, artillery shots, you were only talking about indirect fire?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Now, isn't it true, however, to say that as far as you know that, in Sarajevo, indirect firing or direct firing, the most substantial damage was produced in areas near or around the lines of confrontation?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general, you are correct. However, there are some areas inside Sarajevo which experienced very concentrated fire and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Indeed. Indeed. But I believe that you answered my question. The very last question in relation to the exploitation of misery: You confirmed earlier that there was exploitation of misery; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you think that this exploitation of misery became a political calculation?

utterances.speaker: PYERS TUCKER [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it had to have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. As I said before, this will conclude your testimony in this court. I thank you very much for having come and having answered all the questions of both the parties and the Bench, and I would like to ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, we seek to tender the four documents which are on the exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Two under seal, as far as I see. Madam Registrar, would you please guide us through the documents

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The first document which was tendered the 17th of June, 2002, is Prosecutor's Exhibit 397, under seal, and it is a reported dated 15 November, 1992. We have the second document tendered 17 June, 2002, as Prosecutor's Exhibit 577, under seal, and that is a communications from BH Command dated 24, 25th December, 1992. Prosecutor's Exhibit 530 is an agreement of 13th December, 1992. Prosecutor's Exhibit 653 is a newspaper article of 9 January, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please continue with the Defence exhibits as well? I think it starts with D132.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. Defence Exhibit 132 is S1994/674, annex 6, and it is page 415. Defence Exhibit 133 is S/1994/674, annex 6, page 414.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think the next two, 134 and 135, have the same description but are different pages, that is page 404 and page 405.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. And the last exhibit, D136, is an UNMO briefing dated 16 November, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Since there are no objections, they are all admitted into evidence; 397 and 577 under seal. Mr. Ierace, are you ready to call your next witness? And if -- I can imagine that you would also like to inform the Court, perhaps not today but perhaps at a later stage, about the new scheduling, I don't know whether you prepared it in writing or not, which is usually more efficient in the courtroom. If you would like to present that, I would rather do that at the end of today, let's say the last 10 minutes of today's hearing, and perhaps if you are then still examining the next witness, that you would stop in time in order to have some remaining time to inform the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I will do that Mr. President. I will have copies available. Firstly, I seek the Court's indulgence. Mr. Waespi had a plane to catch and that is why he left earlier. I have present with me Kirsten Cresswell from the OTP, who will assist me with the next witness. Before I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Welcome in the courtroom, Miss Cresswell.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Before I come to the next witness, Mr. President, I understand that the Defence are in some difficulties in relation to their expert attending on Friday to hear the evidence of Mr. Zecevic. I understand further that the difficulty involves him obtaining a visa. I wonder whether the good officers of the Registry may be able to assist in that so as to ensure there is no disruption of the evidence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the visa is the problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I thank the Prosecution for coming to Defence's assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You asked already the intervention of the Registry in order to obtain --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, not yet. I spoke to the Victims and Witness Service and also with the OLAD service and I have spoken to Mr. Ierace, and I wanted to see if worse came to worse, if the witness could be moved to another day. It may happen that it would be possible to obtain a visa for other expert, which I will know either this evening or tomorrow morning. I haven't spoken to the Registry yet, but if that can speed matters up, that we are actively involved in doing this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you ask OLAD to inform, perhaps through the intermediary of the senior legal officer, the Chamber this afternoon on how things are so that we can keep a close eye on it and that we don't waste time on technicalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will do that at the next break.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I call Francis Briquemont.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom. Yes, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would like to avail myself of this opportunity, if that is -- if you would allow me. When we are talking about experts -- I am sorry, the microphone isn't working quite well. Your Honour, I will leave it for the end of our day, after the scheduling. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Briquemont, I presume?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Briquemont, before giving testimony in this court, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. May I invite you to make that declaration. The text will be handed out to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. You may sit down. [In English] Mr. Ierace, please proceed. You will first be examined by counsel for the Prosecution. Examined by Mr. Ierace:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Briquemont, are you a retired general from the Belgian Army?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to the latter part of your -- firstly, did you serve for in excess of 40 years in the Belgian Army before retiring?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: That is right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to the latter part of your military career, were you promoted to the rank of Lieutenant-General on the 26th of March, 1993?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: That is right, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you appointed Commander of the Belgian Intervention Force and Commander-in-Chief of the Belgian forces in Germany on the 29th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On 12 July, 1993, did you take up the position of Commander of the forces of the United Nations in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you remain in that position until the 24th of January, 1994?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In taking up that position, did you take over from General Morillon?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were you succeeded by General Sir Michael Rose?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: Yes, it was General Rose who was my successor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During your tenure as commander, were you based at the forward headquarters in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: I was mainly based in the headquarters in Sarajevo and also in part in Kiseljak where the Main Staff was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your force Commander General Cot from France, and was he based at Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to your man --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I withdraw that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to your mandate, General, please accept that we have heard evidence already as to the mandate of UNPROFOR at other times. Was there a resolution passed by -- adopted by the Security Council on the 4th Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of June, 1993, being Resolution 836, which related to your mandate from the time of the beginning of your tenure?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: Yes. I know Resolution 836 very well, which became very inapplicable for the simple reason that it was a very ambiguous resolution, and on the other hand, what was promised, the means promised by the Security Council, the mission that was designed in Resolution 836, that never arrived to me. So if Mr. President will allow me, I can refer to what I say of the Resolution 836 in the book which I wrote five years ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Before you do that, can I ask you this: Did the resolution refer to certain safe areas in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: Safe areas as defined by the resolution, which I do not have before me, but these were zones of Sarajevo, Srebrenica, Zepa, Tuzla and Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the resolution, as you understood it, authorise the use of force in self-defence by United Nations military forces on the ground?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: Resolution 836 authorised only use of force in legitimate defence, only hypothetically and not only for the safe zones, safe areas.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did you come to the view during your time in Sarajevo in that position that you lacked the necessary military forces to protect United Nations safe areas, including Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, the Resolution 836 designed a kind of a light version, and I never understood that as a General. They said it would be 6.000 men. The only battalion which arrived in the beginning of my mandate was the French Battalion, the 2nd French Battalion, which was deployed in Sarajevo, and much later, parts of a battalion who was called a Nordic battalion, Nordic-Bat. So what we believed or estimated, that only to defend a safe area like Srebrenica, we would need at least a brigade of 3.000 men. So, Mr. Ierace, a lack of resources or forces are flagrant and I never received any reinforcements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, in your dealings with the political and military leadership of the warring parties, did you stratify your command so that certain persons in your command dealt with the same level on both sides or on all sides of the warring parties?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: That is right, Mr. Ierace. As soon as I arrived in Sarajevo, I wanted to be the only interlocutor for the three political leaders and for the three military commanders, for the simple reason that I wanted that we always speak the same language, the same person would be speaking to those who were responsible in political authority. My Chief of Staff did the same with the Chief of Staff of the Serbs, that is General Milovanovic. As far as Sarajevo was concerned, the interlocutory of General Soubirou, or at least from the time of his arrival in Sarajevo in October, was General Galic. And the battalions and battalion commanders were able to have a relationship with local commanders, whether they were Bosnian Serbs -- if you allow me to say Serb, Croat or Muslim, that will be a lot simpler. So with local commanders of the three sides in order to attempt to calm the situation on the ground. Does that answer your question, Mr. Ierace?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. This is just a translation point. On page 59, line 17, the text said, "all sides of the warring parties" or something like that, and that is not -- cannot be interpreted "on both sides of the line." The General spoke of the three chiefs, the three sides, so that would have to be a distinction. Yes, but I have to make this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see, Mr. Briquemont, that you are having difficulties in keeping your earphones on. If you just put them a bit different, it will save you a lot of trouble.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, who were your chiefs of staff during your time in Sarajevo and therefore the officers who dealt with General Milovanovic?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: I had two chiefs of staff. The first one from July to the end of September, beginning of October, was British Brigadier Vere-Hayes, and the second one until the end of my mandate was Brigadier Ramsey.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Given your level of interaction, did you deal with President Karadzic and General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: Yes, I did. And being the only one in Sarajevo, there was a complete absence of political authority. I had to speak to the political leaders and the military leaders. But, yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will firstly ask you some questions about your dealings with President Karadzic. How often did you meet with him?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: It is difficult to answer your question very precisely. I had many meetings with him: the end of July, the beginning of August, when we signed several agreements, and the 30th of July and the 6th of August. In any case, in early August, we signed two others as well. I saw him again at the end of September, when everyone was hoping that the three sides would accept the peace agreement of gentleman Lord Owen and Mr. Stoltenberg, and I saw him again particularly in November and December when the situation was deteriorating again in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And particularly in the -- around Sarajevo, and this was also in relation to the relations that we were trying to establish between the European Community and the Serbs, which were nonexistent until then. And also due to the arrival of Mr. Akashi, who was supposed to take over at the beginning of JNA from Mr. Stoltenberg. Does that answer your question?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It more than answers the question. During the period that you were in that position, can you tell us just briefly what were the significant --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, so that things are clear for the transcript, we do not have question-answer, so perhaps it should be noticed so things are clear

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That would have been something for the small yellow papers, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. But please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the period of your office, can you tell us briefly what were the significant developments, if any, in relation to international attempts to resolve the crisis?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: When I arrived in Sarajevo, the situation was very tense, and General Morillon at the time was trying to establish the limits of the secure areas, areas of security. And during the month of July, I met all of the military and political figures of authority in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and from the 30th of July, in agreement with Mr. Stoltenberg, we tried to calm the situation down on the ground. At the moment when we signed the first agreement at the end of the July, the Serbs had launched a very intense offensive to encircle Mount Igman. It was at that time that Mr. Stoltenberg, who wanted very much to prepare a new agreement, a new peace agreement, asked me to go and negotiate with Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Mladic in order to stop the offensive on Mount Igman, open certain routes and make it so, so that the UN forces can come between the Serbs and the Muslims on Mount Igman. Mr. Stoltenberg asked me at the same time to prepare the military part of the peace agreement that he was hoping to sign as soon as possible. The agreement on Mount Igman was carried out by both parties, including the Serb troops under the command of General Galic. And then we tried throughout August and September to make it so that the operations are stopped on the ground. I can say that in the period in August and in September, we had very high hopes to see this agreement finally signed. The Serbs and the Croats accepted Mr. Stoltenberg and Mr. Owen's agreement, and Mr. Izetbegovic - and I believe that is important that I point this out - before accepting it, asked me to assemble all the leaders, all the Muslim leaders, in Sarajevo. I took the risk because it was a considerable risk to carry out this operation. And it was a great success on the level of security because there were no incidents, but it was a complete defeat because, after this period, Mr. Izetbegovic had the impression that he was able to reconquer, recapture by force, certain territories that were occupied by the Serbs. And if I can summarise my thought, to gain, to win war on the ground, which didn't seem very reasonable. From October, if you allow me to read a few lines written by a journalist from Sarajevo at that moment --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will stop you at that point. You have mentioned some names. Mr. Izetbegovic, his position, what was that?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: Mr. Izetbegovic was the head of the government or, actually, the authority, the Muslim authority. And afterwards was a prime minister. Mr. --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will stop you there. You mentioned also Lord Owen and Mr. Stoltenberg and their efforts to negotiate with the parties. On whose behalf did they carry out those negotiations?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: Mr. Stoltenberg who was the representative of Mr. Boutros-Ghali, who was the United Nations Secretary General, and Lord Owen was the European Union representative. And so they were in charge of the negotiations on behalf of the negotiations and the United Nations and the European Union.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just to intervene, you explained to us that to gain on the ground, which was the wish of Mr. Izetbegovic, it is my recollection that you said that it was practically impossible. But the translation says that it was, which didn't seem very reasonable. It might be that I have wrongly understood you. But did you say that it was not reasonable or it was not possible, in your view?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think in French I said that it wasn't possible. I couldn't see how one party could have the military victory on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to events outside Bosnia-Herzegovina, were there any attempts to bring the parties together in Geneva during that period?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: Mr. Izetbegovic, in the beginning of August, had declared that he would not resume negotiations in Geneva unless an agreement on Mount Igman was signed. I know that before the end of September, that meeting of the three parties on the British Ship, the Invincible, took place, and I know that Mr. Izetbegovic one day went to Geneva, but I don't remember the details of all those meetings, the meetings between Mr. Stoltenberg and Lord Owen and the other parties.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you said that Mr. Izetbegovic in the beginning of August declared that he would not resume negotiations in Geneva. When had negotiations occurred in Geneva previous to August?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: I arrived in early July. The only thing that I can remember here is that in May there was the failure of the negotiations on the Vance-Owen Plan. Mr. Vance left and Mr. Stoltenberg replaced him. But the first objective of Mr. Stoltenberg, and it seemed logical to me, was to try to get a new peace agreement together, which is exactly what happened between Mr. Stoltenberg and Mr. Izetbegovic in May and June. That is what I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I bring you back to the topic of President Karadzic, Mr. Karadzic. You have told us that you frequently met with him. During those meetings, during, in fact, any of those meetings, did he express to you his objective in relation to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: I think that I could say that Mr. Karadzic did not accept the idea that Sarajevo would be a city totally under the domination of the Muslim community. Mr. Karadzic wanted the three communities, that is the Serbs, the Croats and the Muslims, have their say in the management of Sarajevo. And that I could even tell you that at some point there was a mention of dividing Sarajevo in three zones like the way Berlin was. Mr. Karadzic's idea was certainly never to give up Sarajevo only to the Muslims. He wanted the Serbs to have -- he wanted them to have their word to say over what was happening in the capital of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he ever express to you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think I have got to intervene for the transcript. On page 65, line 4, I had the impression that what reads on the line is not exactly what the witness said. There is a problem. Maybe it should be repeated here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have no clear recollection of that part, but I am certain that overnight, specific attention will then be paid to this, although the original is in French. Could you please read, Mr. Briquemont --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is line 4 on page 65. "The first objective of Mr. Stoltenberg."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it is the previous point. I think it is the previous point, but it disappeared from your screen, I take it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I had said before that was that the objective of Mr. Stoltenberg was to recreate the situation that a new peace agreement could be entered into. I don't know if that is exactly what I said, exact words, but that was the idea.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...in mind. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, was it this part of the transcript that was bothering you --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. It was right after that. We can re-check it during the -- I don't want the Prosecution to waste time. I thought I was being helpful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Karadzic express any view as to whether there would be a controlling influence or force on the partitioned or divided Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: I am familiar with the idea of Lord Owen and Mr. Stoltenberg, that is, that the peace agreement of September, and I probably responded to the wishes of the Serb side, they intended to put the city of Sarajevo under UN control, United Nations control, and the city of Mostar under the control of the European Union. That is all that I can tell you about that. However, that was agreed by the two parties, that is in September, by the Serbs and the Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever raise with Dr. Karadzic the issue of the use of artillery by Bosnian Serb forces in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, I can tell you that as --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is a point I've got to come in on the English transcript. On page 67, line 7, I read that it was agreed by the two parties. It said that it was accepted. "Agreed" and "accepted" is not the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness said it was accepted by the Serbs and the Croats. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: I could answer your question. I have it in front of me. There was not a single meeting with Mr. Karadzic or Mr. -- General Mladic. I didn't speak about the problem of using artillery in Sarajevo. My purpose, and the purpose of my entire staff moreover, was also to limit or to try to convince them that the shelling of Sarajevo, especially if the shelling took place in nonmilitary areas, that is civilian areas, then that didn't contribute anything to the Serb cause, but on the contrary, gave them a very, very poor image in the international community. And so I repeat, Mr. Ierace, that constantly throughout the month I was in command, I did not stop raising that problem, but I can tell you that in August and September, we succeeded in limiting as much as possible all that kind of activity on the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any occasion upon which you complained to either Dr. Karadzic or General Mladic about ongoing shelling of civilian areas of Sarajevo when there was any apparent response on the ground to your complaints?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: I think that I said a few minutes ago that when I arrived in Sarajevo, there was great deal of tension, and at the end of July, the 25th of July, or maybe it was the 24th of July, if I remember correctly, even the UN troops were concerned by Serb firing, supposedly an exchange of fire between the Serbs and Muslims, for which Dr. Karadzic apologised in the beginning of August. And so I believe that after September, certain firing began again. If you like, I can explain this type of permanent tension and this constant resumption of activities between Serbs and Muslims in Sarajevo, but I prefer to wait until you ask a question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I am asking you about -- I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, but I've got to come in, Mr. President. Page 68 on line 9, there is a mistake, great mistake in the French booth. We can see that it has to be looked at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I did not follow the French booth. I was reading English.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am doing that for you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, it is approximately time for a break. May I ask, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I am not complaining about the necessity of your interventions, but if you could try to do it in such a way that it is interrupting as little as possible because it is -- sometimes it is necessary, I feel that, but sometimes the way of doing it can make it more easier for Mr. Ierace to continue. We will have a break until five minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, did you ever complain to General Mladic or Dr. Karadzic about shelling of civilian areas while that shelling was still going on, and if so, was there any change in the shelling?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: I can assure you that there were changes in the shelling, certainly during the time August-September --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I can interrupt you there. I am not asking about changing over a period of months, but changes over a period of minutes or hours following a complaint by you.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. Ierace. When we would intervene, frequently noted that the shelling of Sarajevo would diminish or even stop.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: It was a constant intervention on our part. I have already said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask that the witness be shown Exhibit P371.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so. Could the usher assist. Mr. Ierace, it seems as if the Registry has some problems, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: May I continue, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, if you could please answer "yes or no". Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did someone hand you this document?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: Yes, it was given to me at the end of the -- my command period. If I remember correctly, it was by the French medical service in Sarajevo which was in constant contact with the city's hospitals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whereabouts was the French medical service based at that stage, in what building?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: The French medical service basically was deployed at the Sarajevo airport where, each night, there would be casualties and that required an intervention of the French medical teams. And they would -- on a level of the staff, they were at the PTT building, I think it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the casualties that arose each night at the airport civilian casualties or military casualties or both?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: The casualties at the airport essentially were civilian casualties. In fact, they were civilians who were trying to flee from Sarajevo, crossing the airport, but since they were not able to go through the tunnel that went underneath the runway. So it is a very clear answer in respect of the victims; they were essentially civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the source of fire, if you know it, which resulted in the civilian casualties?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: On the Sarajevo airport, there was no question that it was the Serbs who were firing into the access of the runway because they did not accept that the airport could be used by civilians in order to escape from Sarajevo and they would say that that was a neutral zone. So it was an extremely difficult mission for the French Battalion, but the Serbs would fire onto the access of the runway in order to prevent the people -- prevent people from fleeing Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know whether at the places and at the times that the civilians were wounded, there was any source of light?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: The Sarajevo airport was controlled by the French, where they had deployed an infrared camera where they could -- which would enable to spot any movement of civilians. The French were trying, and most of the time they succeeded, they tried to detect this movement of civilians before they would get across the airport fence. And at that point, the person responsible for the airport would set out an alert, set off an alert, which meant that they would go with vehicles to get back -- pick up those civilians and to give them back or to bring them, rather, to the other side of the fence of the airport.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, can you tell us something of the numbers of civilians who were wounded each night whilst trying to cross the airport? I should say wounded or killed.

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: I cannot answer you out of memory but I know that I spent a whole -- I worked with the French for a whole night, and there were two people killed and three or four seriously wounded all through that night. But that is information that you can get, surely, from the French Battalion that was at the airport.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the night that you witnessed this, what were -- what was the type of weaponry used by the Serb forces, in other words, was it rifles, machine-guns, anti-aircraft fire, mortar shells or what?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: Generally, they were bursts of automatic guns or firing, individual shots fired from rifles. I was even fired on by French snipers -- by Serb snipers that evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, as given your position, did you, from time to time, see documentation of numbers of civilian casualties from the -- as a result of civilians crossing the airport at night?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: I myself didn't see those documents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In terms of your observations, did the civilian casualties from that exercise include children?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I bring you now back to the graph in front of you. Having regard to the words on it, did you understand it to be a graphic depiction of the numbers of wounded who were treated at the State Hospital in Sarajevo from January 1993 until December 1993?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: It was shown to me as being that. So that indicates the number of wounded people treated at the hospital between January and December.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any reason to doubt the reliability of the figures indicated at the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: I had no doubts about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Some words in French appear to be handwritten on the graph. Do you know who wrote those words on the graph?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I read them correctly, the words at the bottom of the dip which corresponds to approximately March appear to be shorthand for "conference in Geneva." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please read the other words which appear on the graph, corresponding to early August, 1993?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: The two words are "espoir Geneve."

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Perhaps the translation booth can assist.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That we were hoping, all of us were hoping, all of us in Geneva, that we would be able to sign the peace agreement by Lord Owen and Mr. Stoltenberg. Mr. Ierace, I have to tell you that in Sarajevo I was asked to prepare a room for that agreement to be signed. There was really hope. It was the hope in Geneva as we experienced it then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, were you informed whether the numbers in this graph represent civilian wounded or military wounded, or both?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: I myself always believed that they were both, because when they were wounded, people in the neighbourhoods of Sarajevo where there were -- wounded among the Muslim troops, they were sent to the two city hospitals. And, therefore, in my opinion, that included the civilian and military wounded. That is my opinion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, and please correct me if I am wrong, you are inferring that, you were not told specifically, but you have made a conclusion about the nature of the patients?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: Do you mean that they were civilian and military people? Is that what you mean, Mr. Ierace?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No. I am simply asking if you were, in fact, told, one way or the other, or whether you assume, for the reasons you have indicated, that the figures represent a combination of both?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: It was a personal conclusion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, having regard to the two events during the year, one might conclude that there is a clear relationship between those two events and the degree or rate of casualties in Sarajevo. Are there any observations that you would make about that apparent link or connection?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the French booth is telling me that it didn't understand and would ask Mr. Ierace to repeat the question. I am not sure exactly what was not understood. Perhaps the whole question could be asked again, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I will be happy to do that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is there any -- I withdraw that. Do you believe there to be any correlation between the frequency of casualties in that year and the conference in Geneva in March and the expectations by the parties in August?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, for me, there is no question that the Geneva conference was in May. If you look at the graph, the meeting took place in May in respect of the Vance-Owen Plan, and for me there is no doubt that the lessening of tension was very significant in Sarajevo in August and September before the proposed peace agreement of Lord Owen and Mr. Stoltenberg. So personally, I connect the two elements.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, we heard from you earlier in relation to UN Resolution 836. Did you take any steps by the use of force to limit the use by both sides of snipers where the snipers were deployed against civilians, as you understood it?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: That is right, Mr. Ierace. Especially in October and November, I found it increasingly intolerable to see that the snipers were firing, maybe even just to have fun with the civilians or with the UN people who were crossing the city, or the nongovernmental organisations. The French Battalion, which was deployed in the centre of Sarajevo, in Skanderija, looked for the sniper positions, whether Muslim or Serb. The French Battalion was able to establish or to draw up a map of those positions. We informed the -- Generals Mladic and Delic about that situation which I considered intolerable, and then we carried out some action, and at least in one case, we eliminated a sniper.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From which side -- I rephrase that. On which territory, in terms of the warring parties, was the sniper who was eliminated?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: The sniper was eliminated in the area which was under the control of the Serbs. My objective was at least to send a very clear symbol in order to try to limit the activity of those snipers, and I never had any illusions about the fact that we'd be able to put an end to that activity once and for all simply because not one single political leader, whether Serb, Croat or Muslim, ever came out against that sniper activity in public.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you take any steps to inform General Mladic of the elimination of that Serb sniper or sniper from the Serb territory?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: I don't remember having done that myself. I would simply say the following: That is General Mladic said to me one day, "If one fires on UN people, you can respond to that. That is your right." I don't know whether he was informed, if he was informed by somebody in my staff, but in any case, that was known in Sarajevo and that was the essential thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it your understanding that the sniper position that was fired upon was one from which civilians were shot or United Nations personnel, or both?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: I think that I could say, yes, to your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that it was a position from which --

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: That they were positions from which they could fire either on civilians crossing the city, or UN people, or people from NGOs that were working in the city as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for that. Now, did you ever complain to anyone on the -- either the Bosnian government side or the Bosnian army about them sniping against United Nations personnel?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace. We often complained, but we had no illusions as to the results of the complaints that we were making.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever specifically complain to General Delic about an incident where your car was apparently fired at?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I did complain, Mr. Ierace. I bitterly complained to General Delic because it was certainly the General with whom it was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. easiest to get in touch with, and because it was a Muslim sniper who fired at my car, this unsettled me deeply. Disappointed me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was General Delic at that stage the head of the Bosnian government army?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: Yes. General Delic was certainly the head of the Bosnian army and I would say that he even became -- as time went on, I believe that he had a considerable problem with what we would call mujahedin who came from other countries. They were certainly not Bosniaks. But General Delic was incontestably head of the Muslim army, particularly, specifically when we speak about the end of the year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you form -- withdraw that. Was General Delic someone you met with frequently or infrequently?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: I met General Delic very, very frequently indeed, because his HQ was about 500 metres away from mine in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your dealings with Generals Delic and Mladic, was it important for you or not to assess the degree of reliability that you could place on their word, in other words, whether you could trust them to do what they said they would do?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, I will tell you that with General Delic, I had confidence in what he said, but to start with, at least, he had some difficulties. His subordinates were not carrying out his orders because his armies was constituted a little bit like resistance during the Second World War. For instance, there were no ranks. They were all calling themselves commanders. So General Delic had some problems in terms of establishing a structure of the army. I am speaking professionally. General Mladic, I can tell you that it was very difficult to trust him. But on the contrary, when he gave an order, I could be almost certain that that order would be carried out. And when General Mladic told me in late September, "General, you can assemble your Muslim leaders in Sarajevo," I took the risk. And General Morillon already told me that when Mladic gave an order, then that order was carried out by all of his subordinates.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, did you ever ask General Delic to take steps to ensure that Bosnian government snipers, or snipers operating from territory held by the Bosnian government, did not target UN personnel or civilians?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: Yes I did. I did take these steps. But I always had doubts as to the nature of snipers. I sometimes wondered, but it is just a personal impression, if there were no completely uncontrolled elements, that if you allow me to use this expression, were "playing" at snipers. I was -- admitted that, as far as the commanders were concerned, in a conflict of this type, it was extremely difficult to control the deployment of snipers, moreover, whether this was wanted or not. I told you that already. No political official ever came out in public to stop this activity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you believe or what is your belief as to whether General Delic did what he could to stop that sniping that we have referred to, that is, the sniping of civilians and UN personnel?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: I think that as far as he was concerned, he did make this effort because I have to admit, although I do not have any documents that would allow me to declare this, but it does seem to me, however, that in the last few months, there was always the problem of artillery. But sniping activity did diminish in the end. But that is just a personal impression.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, in relation to General Mladic, from time to time you have told us some things about him, including your belief that his commands were followed. Could you tell us something of his personality in terms of his attitude towards conducting the hostilities against the Bosnian government forces, based on your meetings with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, if I understand the question correctly by Mr. Ierace, it is about a very subjective element linked to a person which is not the accused. And I believe that this kind of consideration which is about a personality of a third person should not be asked as a question in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the relevance of the question is that the Prosecution contends that the accused, General Galic, was subject to the orders of his immediate superior, and that was General Mladic. And given that relationship, questions which go to establishing the intent of General Mladic in relation to the targeting of civilians is directly relevant to the actions of the accused. To spell it out, if General Mladic gave an order that civilians were to be targeted, then the Prosecution case is that General Galic conveyed those orders to his subordinates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but you are asking about personality.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. I am asking about his attitude towards the waging of war and armed conflict, more broadly, against the Bosnian government forces, and that is relevant for the same reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but personality is the first part of your question. Do you think that the witness could give us -- I do understand that you can ask a witness to say something about the attitude, as far as he could learn from this attitude in the way another person expressed himself, and I think you added that to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I did, yes, based on your meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Personality is another thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I take your point, Mr. President. I will amend the question to take that into account. Although I think I did say, "his personality in relation to his attitude." Page 80, line 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I think the relevant words were: "His personality in terms of his attitude."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the transcript it reads: "Could you tell us something of his personality in terms of his attitude." I don't know whether an attitude reflects a personality. But if you could rephrase that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I will, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. It happens that by explaining, at length, his position, Mr. Ierace has already given the element of the answer that he would like to hear from this witness. So the next time, if Mr. Ierace is going to do this, then the witness should not be listening to this. Because now the witness knows what the answer he should give, and that is not really acceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And try to keep the questions as factual as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did General Mladic ever say anything to you which conveyed to you any impression as to his view or attitude towards his enemy or enemies and secondly, the way in which he would conduct hostilities against them?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: I will try and answer in a -- as simply as I can. General Mladic was a professional, a professional of war. He was making war. He wanted to win it. He was incontestably the head of the Serb army. And I never imagined that a Serb officer could either refuse or modify or contest one of his orders. Does that answer your question, Mr. Ierace?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you for that. Now, just before I move on to a different topic, in relation to the civilian casualties at the airport, did that daily occurrence of civilian casualties apply to the entirety of the time that you held your command or only a part or parts of that period of command?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: I can say that as for the problem of Sarajevo airport, lasted throughout my period of command. It was the civilians who were trying to flee Sarajevo. This had nothing to do with the military problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question is whether -- you have told us that civilians were killed or wounded on a nightly basis. Was that daily occurrence -- did that daily occurrence happen throughout your period of command or not?

utterances.speaker: FRANCIS BRIQUEMENT
utterances.text: To say this was a daily occurrence, that would be perhaps exaggerating a little. Throughout my mandate, certainly, and very, very frequently. But I repeat, to have a very precise answer, from Colonel de Richouttz, who was a French officer throughout my period of command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note the time, and would that be convenient?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I am not sure that the name of the Colonel was well pronounced and well transcribed, so perhaps we may need it later. Could the witness repeat the name of his deputy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is Colonel de Richouttz and it is written Romeo -- R-i-c-h-o-u-t-t-z. It is very complicated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Briquemont, since we will have to deal with a few procedural issues for a couple of minutes and since we have to adjourn at a quarter to 2.00, I will ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom and ask you to come back tomorrow morning 9.00, same courtroom, and not to speak with anyone about the testimony you have given in this court and about the testimony that is still to come. So I hope to see you again tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, may I then invite you to ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have seven copies of the timetable for distribution. Mr. President, when everyone has had an opportunity to briefly look at that, I will make a few observations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you. As it presently reads, Ewa Tabeau is to be called on Thursday, the 1st of August and Friday the 2nd of August. If indeed the Trial Chamber does sit on Wednesday, the 10th of July, and perhaps also Friday, the 12th of July, I will move her to those two dates. That will relieve the pressure of the last two weeks, in particular, the last week. Leaving to one side for the moment the issue of 92 bis witnesses, I am confident that with the additional two days from the Plenary, should that happen, that we will finish by Friday, the 2nd of August. I intend to do everything in my power to ensure that witnesses are completed by the dates indicated in the chart. They are the only observations I would make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Of course, the Chamber is quite happy that you managed to make us keen. That fits into the expectations of the Chamber. And I still expect that we could sit on the 10th of July, and if possible, also on the 12th of July, but it is not sure yet. Perhaps we first sleep it over and keep under very strict control that we use not more time than indicated because I wouldn't say that we had a very bad start this week, but we had a start which was not entirely in conformity with the expectations. It started already that the Prosecution took some more time in the examination-in-chief. If the Prosecution sometimes encounters the difficulty of keeping a witness, well, within certain boundaries, as far as time is concerned, of course the Chamber will assist, if requested to do so, by explaining to the witness that we had already a lot of testimony and that if they stick strictly to the answers, that this would be to the benefit of Chamber, the parties, and the witness himself. So if you would need any assistance in this respect, please ask us.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I will, Mr. President. And in relation to the 92 bis application, the Prosecution is assisted by the recent Appeals Chamber judgment in respect to two deceased witnesses Sofi and Kabecic, and in the application of those principals, we have decided to withdraw one of the witnesses and we will shortly file some written submissions in relation to the balance which may be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there at this moment any observation to be made? Yes, Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Prosecution proposal is for Mr. Zecevic, who is scheduled for Friday, for the 21st of June. Of course, if this is possible, if his appearance can be moved to the 29th or the 30th of July, the same time when Mr. Kovac and Mr. Higgs are being moved, being heard at that week. We are proposing this for practical reasons and to save time because in that week when Mr. Zecevic Kovac and Higgs and could be heard, then also the Defence's expert could be present. That would enable our expert, Mr. Milicic [phoen], who is supposed to come on Thursday, then he could hear Mr. Berko and that would help the Prosecution and the Defence. It would help us in a practical way if he could be there starting in the week starting 29th of July. If -- I don't know whether this is possible for the Prosecution to make sure that Mr. Berko comes at the last week of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you discuss this with the Prosecution. I understood this morning that it was mainly a matter of visa for your expert to come. And now there seems to be another problem as well. But I do not know whether the witness or after the witness or expert witness that -- I try to find neutral wordings, whether he did arrive already?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, he hasn't arrived already. However, I would be extremely reluctant to change the timetable. There have been a lot of arrangements put in place, and this is precisely the issue which is causing considerable consternation with the witness unit. Thank you. Mr. President, might I also add that the Defence was first informed that we intended to call Berko Zecevic on this date on the 7th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, Ms. Pilipovic, we will have to take a decision if the parties could not agree. But I understood this morning that it was a mainly a matter of visa for next Friday and not the availability of the expert.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. The expert of the Defence, Mr. Milicic, who is going to be present here when Mr. Berko is being heard, has got a visa and the Defence informed the Registry about this. The only problem would be the arrival of Mr. Milicic because of the Registry organisations in terms of his travel. I don't know whether there are possibilities to alter this. We have submitted our request for travel authorisation, but I don't know whether travel can be authorised for him. The visa doesn't seem to be a problem. The visa is a problem for the expert who is going to be heard for the 24th and 25th of July, but I expect that by that time the Registry will be able to make sure that he gets a visa

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it since we are leaving now on Tuesday that perhaps some extra effort, that travel arrangements should be possible. If you would need the assistance of the Chamber for that after you failed to get it organised, then, please, even just address the matter to the senior legal officer and we will see what we can do. Then I have one minor issue I would like to discuss in closed session and I think two minutes would be enough.
